title: A Salute Returning a Salute
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using the Civil War surrender at Appomattox as its anchor, this piece explores what it means for winners to show grace toward the defeated. When Confederate soldiers marched in to lay down their arms, Union officer Joshua Chamberlain ordered his troops into a posture of respect -- a gesture the opposing general returned in kind. The author uses the episode to argue that gracious losing is a familiar and celebrated virtue, but gracious winning is rarer and more telling of character. Leaders who go out of their way to honor those on the losing side of any contest, the piece argues, reveal something valuable about themselves in the process. The takeaway is a simple standard: give the respect you would want to receive, especially to those who didn't win.
points: At Appomattox, Union officer Joshua Chamberlain ordered his troops to salute the surrendering Confederate soldiers.
Good losers are widely admired, but gracious winners are rarer and more revealing of character.
Showing respect to the defeated carries outsized symbolic weight for everyone watching.
The best leaders extend the same respect to others that they themselves would want to receive.
quotes: A Confederate general riding near the front of the procession appreciated the gesture from Chamberlain and ordered the same posture to be returned by his troops.
The idea of the losing team showing respect for the victors has become deeply ingrained into the ideals of good sportsmanship.
We confer a rare and exalted character to leaders who go out of their way to show respect to those on the losing side.
The best leaders know that the ultimate right to be respected is won by respecting others, especially the vanquished.
In a ceremony at the conclusion of the Civil War, just outside of Appomattox, Virginia, the Confederate Army of the South laid down their weapons before the Union soldiers of the North.
Grant asked 4,000 soldiers to line up at attention on one side of the ceremonial battlefield.
Lee’s defeated infantry units were to march onto the field and place their regimental flags and weapons at the foot of the Union officer in charge.

As the Confederate contingent entered the field, the commanding Union officer, Joshua Chamberlain of Gettysburg fame, told the Union soldiers to “carry arms,” a posture of respect whereby soldiers hold the rifle in their right hand with the muzzle perpendicular to their shoulders.
